title: Psychometric Reliability: Precision and Consistency
description: Explore test-retest, inter-rater, split-half reliability, and internal consistency indexed by Cronbach's alpha.

slides.title: What is Psychometric Reliability? 🎯
slides.content:
# Consistency Across Repeated Measurements

In psychology, **reliability** refers to the consistency, stability, or repeatability of a measurement instrument. A reliable test produces similar results under consistent conditions:

* Under Classical Test Theory:
  **Observed Score = True Score + Measurement Error**
* If measurement error is low, the observed score closely reflects the true underlying construct, and reliability is high.
* A broken bathroom scale that always adds exactly 5 pounds is highly *reliable* (consistent), even though it is completely *invalid* (inaccurate)!

quizData.question: A researcher measures adult intelligence by wrapping a tape measure around their head (cranial circumference). Every time she measures the same person, she gets the exact same measurement of 56 cm. This measure is:

options.text: Both highly reliable and highly valid
Highly reliable, but invalid as a measure of intelligence

quizData.explanation: Head circumference is reliably repeatable (low measurement error), but it does not validly reflect cognitive ability.

slides.title: Four Core Types of Reliability 🔄
slides.content:
## How Psychologists Assess Consistency

| Type of Reliability | How It Is Assessed | When to Use It | Standard Metric |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Test-Retest** | Administer the exact same test to the same group at two different time points | Measuring stable traits (personality, IQ) | Pearson correlation coefficient (r >= 0.70 or 0.80) |
| **Inter-Rater** | Have two or more independent raters score the same behaviors or responses | Observational studies, diagnostic interviews | Cohen's Kappa (categorical) or Intra-class Correlation (ICC) |
| **Internal Consistency** | Correlate responses across all items within a multi-item scale | Multi-item self-report questionnaires | **Cronbach's alpha (α >= 0.70 or 0.80)** |
| **Parallel-Forms** | Administer two equivalent versions of a test designed from the same specifications | Standardized testing (GRE, SAT) to prevent cheating | Correlation between Form A and Form B |

A low Cronbach's alpha indicates that the questions are not measuring a coherent, unified construct.

quizData.question: A psychometrician develops a new 15-item 'Social Anxiety Scale' and calculates Cronbach's alpha as α = 0.42. What does this score indicate?

options.text: The scale has excellent internal consistency
The scale has poor internal consistency; items may be measuring multiple conflicting constructs or contain high noise
The scale is ready for nationwide clinical deployment
The sample size was too large

quizData.explanation: In psychology, Cronbach's alpha should generally exceed 0.70 (and ideally 0.80). An alpha of 0.42 indicates very poor internal consistency.

slides.title: Psychology Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
### Reliability Sets the Ceiling for Validity

Remember this golden psychometric rule:
> *A test can be reliable without being valid, but a test can NEVER be valid unless it is first reliable.*

If your measurement tool is erratic and fluctuates wildly by chance, it cannot possibly measure the true underlying psychological construct!
